title: Database Schema Design, Normalization (1NF–3NF), and Denormalization
learningObjectives: Model entities, relationships, and cardinalities before choosing tables.
Explain update, insert and delete anomalies caused by redundant facts.
Apply 1NF, 2NF and 3NF as practical dependency checks.
Choose between normalization and deliberate denormalization.
Design constraints and indexes that support the intended access patterns.
Explain database schema design, normalization (1nf–3nf), and denormalization using the six-layer interview framework.

mentalModel.text: Imagine storing a customer's address in every order row. When the customer moves, you must update every old order, and missing one creates conflicting addresses. Normalization splits data into tables so each fact is stored in one sensible place and other tables refer to it by key. Sometimes we intentionally copy a value, such as the price charged on an old order, because that value is part of the historical event.

blocks.text: Start by deciding what one row represents and which facts belong to that thing.

First decide what each table represents. A customers table stores customer facts; an orders table stores order facts. If one customer can have many orders, put customer_id on each order. If students can take many courses and each course has many students, use an enrollment table for each student-course relationship.

blocks.title: Many-to-many relationship

blocks.text: The enrollment is a real relationship with its own date and identity rule, not merely a repeated list of course IDs on a student row.

blocks.problem: A student can enroll in many courses, and each course has many students. Each enrollment also has a grade.
reasoning: The relationship is many-to-many, so create an enrollments table with student_id and course_id.
Store grade on the enrollment because it describes that student's participation in that course.
Add a uniqueness rule on the pair if a student may enroll in a course only once.
blocks.outcome: Model a relationship as data when it has its own facts, such as grade, enrollment date, or status.

blocks.text: Redundancy becomes risky when the same fact is copied into several rows that can drift apart.

rows: Update
A supplier address is copied into 200 product rows; changing it updates only 199.
Insert
You cannot record a new supplier until it has at least one product.
Delete
Deleting the last product accidentally removes the only stored copy of the supplier's details.

blocks.text: When the same fact is copied into many rows, changes become risky. If an address is repeated across ten orders, a move requires ten updates. If only nine are changed, the database now tells two different stories. Putting the address in one customer row removes that problem.

blocks.problem: The same instructor name is copied into 200 enrollment rows.
reasoning: When the instructor's name changes, every copy must be updated.
If one row is missed, the database disagrees with itself about the instructor's name.
If instructors are stored only on enrollment rows, a new instructor with no students may be impossible to represent.
blocks.outcome: Update, insertion, and deletion anomalies are signs that facts are stored at the wrong level.

blocks.text: Normalization checks whether a table mixes facts that depend on different things.

Normal forms are checks for whether a table mixes facts that depend on different things. First normal form avoids packing a list into one cell. Second normal form matters when a key has multiple columns: a non-key fact should depend on the whole key, not just one part. Third normal form catches facts that depend on another non-key fact, such as storing a department name on every employee row when department_id already determines it.
A composite-key dependency

Here is a practical way to see the difference. If a row stores `course_ids = '12,18,25'`, the course list is packed into one value: finding one course or enforcing a foreign key becomes awkward. That is the problem 1NF is meant to help avoid—store each relationship as its own row when those values need to be queried and constrained independently.

Now consider `Enrollment(student_id, course_id, student_name, course_title, grade)` with `(student_id, course_id)` as the key. `student_name` depends only on `student_id`, and `course_title` depends only on `course_id`; those are partial dependencies, the issue 2NF addresses for composite keys. If `course_id` determines `instructor_id`, and `instructor_id` determines `instructor_name`, storing `instructor_name` on every enrollment adds a transitive dependency—the kind of problem 3NF helps remove.

reasoning: If the title is stored only in the courses table, one row needs updating.
If it is copied into every enrollment, every copy must be updated correctly or reports disagree.
Keep course facts with the course; keep enrollment-specific facts such as grade on the student-course relationship.
blocks.outcome: Use normal forms to find facts stored at the wrong grain. The goal is consistent data and clear ownership, not normalization for its own sake.
blocks.problem: A course changes its title, but the title is copied into 400 enrollment rows.

blocks.title: Normal forms are not a substitute for dependency analysis
blocks.content: Do not normalize by slogan. Identify functional dependencies and candidate keys, then decide which table should own each fact. A JSON column is not automatically denormalized or unnormalized; its suitability depends on the domain and access patterns.

blocks.text: A normalized model separates current product facts from facts about what was purchased at a particular time.

blocks.title: Orders and line items

blocks.text: A line item should store quantity and the price charged at purchase time. The product table stores today's catalog price, which may change later. The order's unit_price is not a mistake just because the number appears twice: it records what the customer was actually charged.

blocks.problem: A product currently costs $20, but a customer bought it last year for $15.
reasoning: products.price represents the current catalog price.
order_items.unit_price records the price charged for that purchase.
If the catalog price changes tomorrow, historical order totals should not silently change.
blocks.outcome: Some duplication is intentional when it records a historical snapshot. Define what the duplicated value means.

blocks.text: Denormalization deliberately stores a duplicate or precomputed value to make a measured workload faster; it adds a consistency responsibility.

Denormalization means deliberately copying or precomputing data to make an important read faster or simpler. A dashboard might store a daily sales total instead of adding millions of orders on every page load. That total can become stale, so the system needs a clear update and repair process.

rows: Compute with JOIN/aggregate at read time
One authoritative source; freshest committed data.
Read query may be expensive at scale.
Persist a derived column
Fast point reads and simple API response.
Every write path must keep the derived value correct; backfills and repairs are needed.
Materialized view or summary table
Efficient analytical reads and batch refresh options.
Refresh/maintenance complexity and potentially stale results.
Cache/search projection
Tailored read model for high-volume access.
Eventual consistency, replay, reconciliation and operational overhead.

blocks.text: Denormalize only after measuring a real bottleneck and defining the consistency contract. Start with the normalized model because it is easier to reason about, then add a projection when evidence justifies it.

blocks.problem: A dashboard repeatedly sums 50 million order rows to display today's revenue.
reasoning: Measure the query and confirm repeated aggregation is the real bottleneck.
A daily summary table may make reads much cheaper, but it must handle new, cancelled, refunded, and corrected orders.
Define whether the dashboard may be briefly stale and how to rebuild or reconcile the summary.
blocks.outcome: Denormalize only when the read benefit justifies the extra storage and there is a clear plan to keep the value correct.

concepts.title: Reviewing a schema against real queries

blocks.text: Review a schema against real reads, writes, and business rules rather than designing from table names alone.

For each important query, write down what it filters, which tables it joins, what one result row represents, how often the data changes, and how fast the query needs to be. Then choose constraints and indexes to support it. Don't duplicate data just because a column appears in a query.

blocks.title: Avoid premature denormalization
blocks.content: A copied field creates a synchronization contract even if no one writes that contract down. If the source changes and the copy does not, the system now has two conflicting answers.

blocks.problem: An endpoint lists the newest 20 orders for one customer and includes the customer's current name.
reasoning: The query filters orders by customer_id and orders by created_at.
An index beginning with customer_id and then created_at may support that access pattern.
Keep customer name in customers and join it when needed unless measurements justify a maintained copy.
blocks.outcome: Model facts correctly first, then optimize the queries the application actually runs.

concepts.title: Worked exercise: normalize an enrollment table

blocks.text: Use dependencies to decide where facts belong; don't normalize just to follow a rule mechanically.

Start with Enrollment(student_id, student_name, course_id, course_title, instructor_id, instructor_name, grade), where (student_id, course_id) identifies one enrollment. student_id determines student_name; course_id determines course_title and instructor_id; instructor_id determines instructor_name. Those rules tell us which facts belong together.

blocks.title: Functional dependencies
rows: student_id → student_name
Student facts depend only on student identity
course_id → course_title, instructor_id
Course facts depend only on course identity
instructor_id → instructor_name
Instructor name depends on instructor identity
(student_id, course_id) → grade
Grade depends on the full enrollment key

blocks.text: The original table repeats student, course, and instructor facts. Updating an instructor name requires changing every enrollment row for that instructor; a new course cannot be recorded until a student enrolls; deleting the last enrollment can erase course details. These are update, insert, and delete anomalies.

blocks.problem: Enrollment(student_id, student_name, course_id, course_title, instructor_id, instructor_name, grade) has key (student_id, course_id).
reasoning: student_name depends on student_id; course_title and instructor_id depend on course_id; instructor_name depends on instructor_id.
Move students, courses, and instructors into their own tables and let enrollments refer to them.
Keep grade in enrollments because it depends on the student-course relationship.
blocks.outcome: Each table now stores facts about one entity or relationship, reducing inconsistent copies while preserving the ability to query through joins.

blocks.title: Normalization is about dependencies, not visual duplication
blocks.content: The current catalog price and the historical unit price charged on an order line are different facts, even if their values happen to match.

blocks.text: 1. Problem and motivation — When the same fact is copied into multiple rows, one update can change only some copies. These update, insert, and delete anomalies are data-modeling problems, not merely messy code.

2. Definition and design choice — Normalization separates facts according to their dependencies so each fact has an appropriate home. Denormalization deliberately duplicates or precomputes data when measured read patterns justify the added consistency work.

steps.title: Identify entities and dependencies
steps.description: Determine which attributes describe a customer, order, product, or relationship.

steps.title: Choose keys
steps.description: A candidate key uniquely identifies a row; functional dependencies show which attributes depend on which keys.

steps.title: Separate independent facts
steps.description: Move repeated product or customer facts into their own relations and reference them with foreign keys.

steps.title: Validate query and write paths
steps.description: Check joins, transaction boundaries, and reporting needs; denormalize only with a refresh or consistency strategy.

blocks.problem: If every order row stores the product name, renaming a product requires updating many historical orders and can leave inconsistent copies. A normalized product table avoids that anomaly; a reporting snapshot may still intentionally store a product-name-at-purchase value because historical meaning differs from the current product name.
reasoning: Normalize facts that must stay consistent, but distinguish current attributes from historical snapshots. The right schema follows business meaning and invariants, not a rule to minimize joins at all costs.
Check the actual query shape, data distribution, concurrency, and database-engine behavior before generalizing the result.
blocks.outcome: Normalize facts that must stay consistent, but distinguish current attributes from historical snapshots. The right schema follows business meaning and invariants, not a rule to minimize joins at all costs.

blocks.title: 5. Anti-pattern to avoid
blocks.content: Do not denormalize just because joins exist, and do not normalize historical facts so aggressively that a past transaction changes meaning when a current entity changes.

blocks.prompt: 6. Interview probe — When is storing a duplicated value in an order table correct rather than a normalization mistake?
blocks.answer: When it captures a historical fact that must remain stable, such as the price or product description shown at purchase time. Document that meaning and decide how it differs from the current catalog value.
blocks.explanation: Normalization is about dependencies and anomalies. Intentional snapshots are valid when they represent a different business fact.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Normalization versus read simplicity
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content:
Trade-off: Normalization reduces inconsistent copies and clarifies ownership; denormalization can reduce joins and improve hot reads.

Failure mode: A derived copy becomes stale because one write path failed to update it.

Decision rule: Normalize first. Denormalize only for a measured access-pattern need and specify update ownership, staleness, reconciliation and backfill behavior.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Natural business fact versus historical snapshot
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content:
Trade-off: Referencing the current product price avoids duplication; storing the price charged on an order preserves transaction history.

Failure mode: Old invoices change when the product's current price changes.

Decision rule: Ask whether the field describes current state or a historical event. Historical transaction facts often need immutable snapshots.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: One table versus junction table
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content:
Trade-off: A list embedded in a row can be convenient for bounded, aggregate-owned children; a junction table supports independent relationships, constraints and querying.

Failure mode: A delimited/list field makes referential integrity and querying fragile, or a junction table is introduced for data that never needs independent identity without a clear benefit.

Decision rule: Model cardinality and lifecycle. Use a junction table for many-to-many relationships and for relationships with meaningful attributes.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Strict normalization versus performance
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content:
Trade-off: More normalized schemas may require joins; denormalized read models can lower read cost at the expense of consistency complexity.

Failure mode: The team optimizes a hypothetical join cost and creates a difficult distributed consistency problem.

Decision rule: Measure query plans and workload first. Keep authoritative data normalized and make projections rebuildable where possible.

tradeoffsAndPitfalls.title: Nullable attributes versus explicit state
tradeoffsAndPitfalls.content:
Trade-off: NULL is compact for optional facts; explicit state modeling is clearer when different absence reasons imply different behavior.

Failure mode: A single nullable timestamp is interpreted as several incompatible lifecycle states.

Decision rule: Use explicit statuses when operational meaning differs; constrain which fields are valid in each state.

revisionSheet.text:
What problem does normalization primarily address?

Answer: Redundant facts that create update, insert and delete anomalies and inconsistent copies.

What is a functional dependency?

Answer: A relationship where a set of attributes determines another attribute, written X → Y. It helps identify where facts belong.

What does 2NF rule out?

Answer: Partial dependency of a non-prime attribute on part of a candidate key; this is most relevant with composite candidate keys.

What is the informal 3NF intuition?

Answer: Non-key facts should depend on the key, the whole key, and not on another non-key fact; formal definitions use functional dependencies and candidate keys.

Does normalization prohibit storing a product price in an order line?

Answer: No. The order-line price may be the historical price charged, a different fact from the product's current catalog price.

When is denormalization reasonable?

Answer: When a measured access pattern justifies it and the team defines consistency, updates, repair and backfill behavior.

What should you define before designing a table?

Answer: What one row represents, its identity, relationships, functional dependencies, and lifecycle.

What does a many-to-many relationship usually require?

Answer: A junction/association table with foreign keys, a uniqueness rule, and any attributes that belong to the relationship.

questions.prompt: A table stores student_name and course_title on each enrollment row, keyed by (student_id, course_id). What is the main modeling issue?

options.text: The names depend on parts of the composite key, creating redundancy.
Foreign keys cannot reference composite keys.
Every table must have exactly one column.
Normalization always requires JSON.

questions.explanation: Student facts depend on student_id and course facts on course_id, not on the full enrollment key. Separate those entities.

questions.prompt: Why might an order line store unit_price even though products has a current price?

options.text: To avoid every foreign key.
Because it may record the historical price charged at purchase time.
Because normalization forbids product references.
Because numeric columns cannot be joined.

questions.explanation: Historical transaction price and current catalog price represent different facts.

questions.prompt: What should be decided before introducing a denormalized summary?

options.text: Which component owns updates to the summary.
Acceptable staleness and repair strategy.
How backfills and reconciliation will work.
That duplicated data can never become inconsistent.

questions.explanation: Denormalization creates a consistency obligation. Ownership, staleness, backfill and repair must be explicit.

questions.prompt: Normalization means never storing the same-looking value in two tables.
questions.explanation: The values may represent different facts, such as current catalog price and historical price charged. Analyze dependencies and meaning.

questions.prompt: A report joins raw orders to raw order_items and raw payments, then sums orders.total_amount. Each order has multiple items and payment attempts. Why can the total be wrong?

options.text: SUM removes duplicates automatically.
Independent one-to-many joins multiply each order row; aggregate child relations to the required grain before joining.
Store order totals on every payment row.
DISTINCT on the final sum fixes every duplication.

questions.explanation: Independent one-to-many joins can produce item-count × payment-count rows per order, repeating order totals. Pre-aggregate child relations to one row per order.

questions.prompt: In Enrollment(student_id, course_id, student_name, course_title, grade), assume the key is (student_id, course_id), student_id determines student_name, and course_id determines course_title. Which issue violates 2NF?

options.text: grade depends on the whole composite key
student_name and course_title depend on only part of the composite key
student_id is a foreign key
course_id is numeric

questions.explanation: Second normal form rules out partial dependency of non-prime attributes on part of a candidate key. Student and course facts belong with their own entities.

questions.prompt: Which statements about normalization and denormalization are sound? Select all that apply.

options.text: Normalization helps reduce update, insert, and delete anomalies.
Every repeated-looking value is necessarily redundant.
Denormalized copies require an explicit consistency and repair strategy.
A historical price charged on an order line can be a different fact from today's catalog price.

questions.explanation: Normalization follows dependencies and meaning. Some repeated values represent separate historical facts; denormalized read models need clear update ownership and repair.

questions.prompt: Third normal form informally asks that non-key facts depend on the key, the whole key, and not on another non-key fact.
questions.explanation: This is a useful interview intuition for 3NF, although formal definitions are stated in terms of functional dependencies and candidate keys.

questions.prompt: A system must preserve the exact amount charged on an invoice even after the product catalog price changes. Where should the charged unit price live?

options.text: Only in the current products.price column
On the order line as a historical transaction fact, with a product reference
In an application cache only
In a trigger that rewrites old invoices to today's price

questions.explanation: The charged price is part of the historical transaction. It differs semantically from the current catalog price and should be preserved on the order line.

questions.prompt: Before adding a denormalized customer-revenue summary table, what should the team decide? Select all that apply.

options.text: Which process owns updates to the summary.
The tolerated staleness and how consumers learn about it.
How backfills, reconciliation, and repair happen.
That summary values cannot ever diverge from source rows.

questions.explanation: A summary table is a second representation of derived facts. It needs update ownership, freshness expectations, backfill, reconciliation, and repair procedures.

questions.prompt: A table stores one row per student-course enrollment. A student can enroll in many courses, and a course can have many students. Which design best models the relationship?

options.text: Store a comma-separated list of course IDs in students.
Duplicate the student's full row for every course and omit a key.
Use an enrollment junction table with student_id, course_id, a uniqueness rule, and relationship attributes such as grade.
Use a single nullable column that alternates between student and course IDs.

questions.explanation: A junction table models the many-to-many relationship and holds facts about the relationship itself, such as grade or enrollment date.

questions.prompt: Normalization always means a query can never need a JOIN.
questions.explanation: Normalization separates facts according to dependencies, which often means queries join related relations. The trade-off is less update anomaly risk versus query complexity and possible read cost.

interviewScenarios.prompt: Design a schema for orders and line items where product prices can change but invoices must remain historically accurate. Explain normalization and any deliberate duplication.
strongAnswerPoints: Separate customers, orders, products and order_items by entity and grain.
Use foreign keys and a stable line identity or composite key.
Store quantity and the unit price actually charged on the order line.
Explain why the transaction price is a historical fact, not a redundant copy of today's catalog price.
Define currency, discounts, tax, refunds and rounding semantics if relevant.
Avoid denormalizing unrelated current customer fields unless a snapshot is a business requirement.
pitfalls: Joining old invoices to the current product price.
Treating every repeated value as invalid redundancy.
Ignoring currency, discounts or tax rules.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would model orders and order_items separately, with a product reference on each line. The product table holds current catalog price; the order line stores the unit price charged at purchase time, because that value is part of the historical transaction. That is not merely a duplicated current fact. I would constrain positive quantity and valid amounts, define how discounts, tax and currency are recorded, and use foreign keys to preserve relationships. I would only add further read-model duplication if measured query needs justify it and its consistency contract is explicit.

interviewScenarios.prompt: An order service needs fast customer-order history and immutable invoice totals. Propose a normalized write model and any justified read-model duplication, explaining the consistency contract.
strongAnswerPoints: Identify row grain and entities such as customers, orders, order_items, and products.
Keep current product facts separate from historical line prices and invoice snapshots that represent transaction-time facts.
Use keys, foreign keys, and row-level constraints for durable invariants.
Only denormalize after identifying a measured read bottleneck and the required freshness target.
Define update ownership, idempotent rebuild/backfill, reconciliation, and repair for derived summaries.
Explain how transaction boundaries preserve invoice totals across order-line writes.
pitfalls: Recomputing old invoice values from current catalog prices.
Duplicating customer or product facts without update ownership.
Treating eventual consistency as acceptable without a stated freshness contract.
interviewScenarios.referenceAnswer: I would keep customers, orders, order_items, and products as separate entities, with each order line preserving the unit price and relevant tax/discount facts charged at purchase time. A transaction should create the order, lines, and invoice snapshot consistently. For a history dashboard, I would first measure the query and index the normalized model appropriately. If a denormalized customer-order summary is still justified, I would define its owner, freshness target, idempotent rebuild, backfill and reconciliation process, and what happens when updates fail. That preserves a clear source of truth while allowing a deliberate read optimization.

description: Database Schema Design, Normalization (1NF–3NF), and Denormalization. Interview-focused explanations, worked examples, trade-offs, and practice.
